conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Maya, and I’m the perinatal mental-health clinician here. I’ll be guiding you through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s a short, well-studied questionnaire that helps us understand how moms are feeling emotionally in the first weeks and months after birth.  

Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team involved in your care; nothing is shared outside unless safety requires it. We simply want to make sure you feel heard and supported.  

I’ll ask you ten questions about how you’ve felt in the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is most true for you. Ready to start?  

Here’s the first one:  
Over the past week, when you were able to choose, have you found enjoyment in things—the little pleasures like a warm drink, a favorite show, or a friend’s text—or has even that felt flat or absent?

I guess… most things feel kind of flat. I’ll still make myself a cup of tea or scroll through a show, but it’s like I’m doing it because I know I used to like it—not because it actually feels good now. It just seems pointless a lot of the time.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not really… I mean, every now and then the baby will do something that makes me crack a tiny smile, but I haven’t actually laughed in days. Even when my partner tries to joke with me, it feels like I’m too tired or worried to find it funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Honestly, no… I can’t remember the last time I felt excited about anything. I’ll tell myself, “Tomorrow we’ll go for a walk” or “I’ll video-chat my best friend,” but when the moment comes I just feel blank—like, what’s the point? Even little outings with the baby feel like chores, not something to look forward to.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If he spits up more than usual, I immediately think it’s because I ate the “wrong” thing or didn’t burp him long enough. Last night he was fussy for two hours and I kept replaying every little choice—was it the bath temperature, did I not soothe him right? I ended up crying because it feels like I’m failing him somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty often… my mind just keeps jumping to the worst-case thing. Like, I’ll watch him sleep and suddenly worry he’s stopped breathing, so I have to put my hand on his chest. Or I’ll think the stroller wheel is going to come off and the whole thing will tip into traffic. I know it sounds crazy, but in the moment it feels so real, and I can’t shake it until I check everything three times.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes, yeah. Out of nowhere my heart starts racing and I feel like I can’t get enough air—like something awful is about to happen, even if I’m just sitting on the couch. It usually passes after a few minutes, but in that moment I’m convinced there’s danger and I need to run or hide, even though I couldn’t tell you what I’m scared of.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most days it feels like the pile never shrinks. Feed, change, rock, laundry, dishes—then he’s crying again before I’ve even had a sip of water. I keep thinking, “If I just push through, it’ll feel manageable,” but it never really does. I haven’t used anything to cope—no wine, no pills—I just keep trudging, but it’s like I’m stuck in sand.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I have, yeah. I finally get him down, but then I lie there with my mind racing—did I sterilize the bottles right, is he gaining enough weight, will I ever feel like myself again? Some nights I drop off okay, then jolt awake at 2 a.m. and can’t get back to sleep. It’s like the sadness and the worries just swirl around every time the room is quiet.
I have felt sad or miserable

That’s most of the day, honestly. I wake up already feeling heavy, like there’s this gray cloud hanging over everything. Even when the baby smiles, the sadness is still right there in my chest. I keep waiting for it to lift, but it just lingers, and sometimes it feels like I’m watching life happen through a window.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened three or four times this week. Yesterday I burst into tears while folding his onesies because they looked so tiny and I suddenly felt like I wasn’t doing enough for him. Other times I’ll just be rocking him and the tears start rolling—no real trigger, just this wave of sadness that won’t stay inside.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I feel low and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom he needs.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum parent (partner present) – infant approx. 2–4 wks old  
Date: [today]  
Clinician: [licensed MH professional]

A. Responses consistent with:
1. Persistent low mood, anhedonia, tearfulness (Q1, Q2, Q8, Q9)  
2. Marked guilt / self-blame regarding infant care (Q3)  
3. Generalized & postpartum-specific anxiety, panic symptoms, repetitive safety-checking (Q4, Q5)  
4. Subjective overwhelm, sense of “stuckness,” no maladaptive coping substances used (Q6)  
5. Mood-congruent insomnia (initial & middle) (Q7)

B. Positive screening indicators for probable postpartum depression ± comorbid anxiety:
- EPDS-like items: 9/10 endorse distress; severity appears moderate–high  
- Functional impact: impaired sleep, feeding/care routines perceived as unmanageable, reduced bonding enjoyment  
- No current self-harm ideation (Q10 denies); nevertheless, safety plan reviewed and emergency contacts provided

C. Risk factors noted:
- First-time parenting, self-criticism, absence of “relief” moments, limited expressed support beyond partner  
- No suicidal ideation; no psychotic features; no substance misuse

D. Screening conclusion:
High likelihood of postpartum depressive episode with comorbid anxiety features; parental distress significantly above normal postpartum adjustment. Recommend expedited referral to perinatal mental health specialist for comprehensive evaluation and evidence-based intervention (CBT or medication consult). Provide printed/postpartum crisis line and schedule follow-up within 1 week to reassess mood, coping, and infant safety.
